title: CA Final Advanced Financial Management (AFM) – Complete Theory Quick Recall Master Sheet
purpose: 20-mark theory target: convert probable descriptive concepts into quick-recall definitions, keywords, memory codes and answer skeletons.
important_note: All questions from the user's existing keyword sheet are retained and mapped to the corresponding current ICAI 15-chapter structure. Additional concept questions are added from the ICAI AFM syllabus, Saransh Last Mile Referencer and 2025 study material so that the sheet is comprehensive without becoming a textbook.

answer_method.ideal_3_to_5_mark_answer: Definition/meaning → 4–6 keywords → one-line explanation of each keyword → conclusion.
answer_method.ideal_6_to_8_mark_answer: Meaning → classification/features → 5–7 explained points → formula/diagram wherever relevant → conclusion.
answer_method.recall_rule: Do not memorise paragraphs. Memorise the MEMORY CODE first, then expand every letter into one sentence.
answer_method.exam_trigger: If the question asks 'explain', 'discuss', 'state features', 'enumerate', 'differentiate' or 'what are', use the definition + keywords + explanation format.

chapter_mapping_note.user_sheet_chapters: The existing sheet uses a different chapter numbering sequence. Its topics have been preserved and mapped to the current ICAI 15-chapter structure.
chapter_mapping_note.official_current_structure: 1 Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy; 2 Risk Management; 3 Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions; 4 Security Analysis; 5 Security Valuation; 6 Portfolio Management; 7 Securitization; 8 Mutual Funds; 9 Derivatives Analysis and Valuation; 10 Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management; 11 International Financial Management; 12 Interest Rate Risk Management; 13 Business Valuation; 14 Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring; 15 Startup Finance.

chapters.title: Financial Policy and Corporate Strategy
chapters.memory_map: CORPORATE → FINANCIAL PLANNING → FINANCIAL DECISIONS → CFO → SGR → EFR

questions.question: Corporate Level Strategy and the three basic questions
questions.definition: Corporate-level strategy decides which businesses the organisation should be in and how the overall portfolio of businesses should be managed.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain corporate strategy → selection of businesses → test every strategic choice through Suitability, Feasibility and Acceptability.

questions.question: Financially Sustainable Organisation
questions.definition: A financially sustainable organisation is capable of continuing its activities over time through diversified income, sound systems, financial autonomy and clear values.
questions.answer_skeleton: Start with continuity → diversify income → plan regularly → maintain systems → build credibility → preserve value clarity → achieve financial autonomy.

questions.question: Outcomes of Financial Planning
questions.definition: Financial planning translates organisational objectives into financial decisions and measurable financial outcomes.
questions.answer_skeleton: State the three outcomes and explain that planning links goals with decisions and measurable results.

questions.question: Strategy at different hierarchy levels
questions.definition: Strategy operates at corporate, business-unit and functional/departmental levels, with each level answering a different management question.
questions.answer_skeleton: Corporate = where to compete; Business = how to compete; Functional = how each function supports execution.

questions.question: Key Financial Strategy Decisions
questions.definition: Financial strategy determines how funds are raised, invested, distributed and managed across investments.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each decision in one line: raise funds, deploy funds, distribute earnings and manage portfolio investments.

questions.question: Interface of Financial Policy and Strategic Management
questions.definition: Financial policy supports strategic management by ensuring that strategic choices have appropriate financing, investment and distribution decisions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Strategy determines direction → finance provides resources → capital structure, investment allocation and dividend policy support execution.
questions.exam_trigger: Interface between financial policy and strategic management

questions.question: Role of CFO in the post-pandemic environment
questions.definition: The modern CFO is not limited to accounting; the role extends into strategic decisions, risk, operations, restructuring and sustainable financing.
questions.answer_skeleton: Begin with strategic CFO → explain risk, supply chain, M&A/restructuring and ESG financing responsibilities.

questions.question: Financial Goals versus Sustainable Growth
questions.definition: Sustainable growth means expanding sales and operations at a rate consistent with profitability, asset utilisation, financing capacity and financial policies.
questions.answer_skeleton: Sales growth creates funding requirements → growth must remain consistent with operating and financial policies → aim for stable sustainable expansion.

questions.question: Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) and assumptions
questions.definition: SGR represents the maximum sales growth that can be supported without raising additional external equity/borrowing beyond the assumed financing structure.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define SGR → give formula → explain ROE and retention → state assumptions regarding capital structure, payout and financing.

questions.question: External Funding Requirement (EFR) approaches
questions.definition: EFR estimates the additional external funds required to support projected growth after considering internally generated funds and spontaneous financing.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define EFR → Analytical approach = project individual balance-sheet items → Formula approach = use relationship-based formula.

chapters.title: Risk Management
chapters.memory_map: RISK TYPES → VAR → COMPLIANCE/OPERATIONS → COUNTERPARTY → COUNTRY → IMPORTER

questions.question: Identification of Financial Risk and Currency Risk
questions.definition: Financial risk arises from adverse financial-market or financing conditions; currency risk arises from adverse exchange-rate movements affecting foreign-currency positions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify each risk → explain the event causing it → state the possible financial consequence.

questions.question: Applications of Value at Risk (VaR)
questions.definition: VaR estimates the potential maximum loss of a portfolio over a specified time horizon at a specified confidence level under normal market conditions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define VaR → explain how it quantifies loss → list five managerial applications.

questions.question: Compliance Risk and Operational Risk
questions.definition: Compliance risk is the risk of violating applicable rules and regulations; operational risk arises from failures in internal people, processes or day-to-day operations.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → distinguish external regulatory consequences from internal operational failures.

questions.question: Counterparty Risk Management
questions.definition: Counterparty risk management controls the possibility that the other party to a financial transaction fails to meet its contractual obligation.
questions.answer_skeleton: Check counterparty → limit exposure → monitor → act quickly → obtain protection where appropriate.

questions.question: Main Features of VaR
questions.definition: VaR is a statistical risk measure that expresses a potential worst-case loss as a monetary or percentage amount for a defined probability and horizon.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → specify amount/percentage → confidence/probability → horizon → statistical basis → Z-score.

questions.question: Stakeholder View of Financial Risk
questions.definition: Financial risk affects stakeholders differently because each stakeholder has a different exposure to the organisation's financial condition.
questions.answer_skeleton: Shareholders/lenders → company → government; explain how risk affects return, solvency and public/revenue interests.

questions.question: Country Risk Assessment and Mitigation
questions.definition: Country risk is the possibility that political, economic or country-specific conditions adversely affect an international investment or transaction.
questions.answer_skeleton: Assess political and macro conditions → reduce dependence through local sourcing/JVs/local financing.

questions.question: Risks faced by an Importer-Manufacturer
questions.definition: An importer-manufacturer is exposed to multiple risks because it imports inputs, processes them domestically and sells the output, often across markets.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify the four risks and link each to the import, manufacturing or sales chain.

questions.question: Current trends/factors affecting Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: Modern capital budgeting recognises that project cash flows are affected by changing economic, technological and governmental conditions.
questions.answer_skeleton: State why traditional certainty assumption is unrealistic → explain inflation, technology and government-policy effects.

questions.question: Impact of Inflation on Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: Inflation affects project revenues, operating costs and the real value of tax-related cash flows, so cash flows and discount rates must be treated consistently.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain inflation → revenues/costs rise → depreciation tax shield may not rise proportionately → real return is affected.

questions.question: Risk versus Uncertainty
questions.definition: Risk exists when variability of outcomes can be assessed and probabilities can be assigned; uncertainty exists when probabilities cannot be reliably assigned.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → explain measurement difference → state why risk adjustment is required.

questions.question: Internal and External Factors affecting Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: Project cash flows are influenced by project/company-specific internal risks and broader macroeconomic external risks.
questions.answer_skeleton: Internal = project/company factors; external = macroeconomic and policy factors.

questions.question: Methods of Incorporating Risk in Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: Risk-adjustment methods modify either expected cash flows or discount rates to reflect project risk.
questions.answer_skeleton: Classify statistical and conventional methods → explain how each incorporates risk.

questions.question: Adjusted Present Value (APV)
questions.definition: APV separates the value of the project under all-equity financing from the present value of financing side effects such as tax benefits.
questions.answer_skeleton: Value project independently → calculate financing effects → add present value of relevant benefits/costs.

questions.question: Optimum Replacement Cycle
questions.definition: Optimum replacement analysis determines the economically appropriate replacement timing by comparing annualised/equivalent costs or benefits over alternative lives.
questions.answer_skeleton: Compare alternative replacement cycles → convert to comparable annual measure → select the economically appropriate cycle.

chapters.title: Security Analysis
chapters.memory_map: FUNDAMENTAL → TECHNICAL → EMH → MARKET INDICATORS → TESTS

questions.question: Technical Analysis in an Efficient Market
questions.definition: Technical analysis attempts to use price/volume patterns to identify future price movements, while efficient-market theory questions whether such patterns can consistently generate abnormal returns.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain technical analysis → crowd psychology → gradual demand/supply adjustment → efficiency makes exploitable patterns self-defeating.

questions.question: Principles of Technical Analysis
questions.definition: Technical analysis rests on the idea that market prices incorporate relevant information, prices move in trends and historical market behaviour can recur.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain all three principles separately.

questions.question: Market Indicators
questions.definition: Market indicators are statistical or market-based measures used to assess market direction, participation, sentiment and relative performance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name each indicator → state what aspect of market behaviour it measures.

questions.question: Factors affecting Economic Analysis
questions.definition: Economic analysis evaluates the broad economic environment before assessing industries and securities.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each factor and its potential effect on corporate earnings/market conditions.

questions.question: Factors affecting Industry Analysis
questions.definition: Industry analysis examines the structural attractiveness and competitive conditions of an industry.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain life cycle → demand/supply → entry barriers → government → competition.

questions.question: Challenges to Efficient Market Theory
questions.definition: Efficient-market theory can face practical challenges because investors and markets may not always have complete information or process it rationally.
questions.answer_skeleton: State each challenge → explain how it may prevent perfect information efficiency.

questions.question: Tests for Weak-form Efficiency
questions.definition: Weak-form efficiency concerns whether historical price and return information is already reflected in current prices.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define weak form → explain what each test checks → conclude how randomness relates to weak-form efficiency.

questions.question: Moving Average Buy/Sell Signals
questions.definition: Moving-average analysis compares market price with its moving-average line to generate trend-based signals.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain upward/downward crossings and interpret them in the context of the direction of the moving average.

chapters.title: Security Valuation
chapters.memory_map: RETURN → ERP → DISCOUNT → EQUITY → PREFERENCE → DEBT → VALUER

questions.question: Meaning/Overview of Valuation
questions.definition: Valuation estimates the intrinsic worth of an asset by assessing expected future benefits, risk, timing and appropriate required return.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define valuation → explain intrinsic value → connect future benefits with risk and discounting.

questions.question: Required Rate of Return
questions.definition: Required return is the minimum return an investor expects for committing funds to an asset of a specified risk.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain opportunity cost → relate to risk and cost of capital.

questions.question: Equity Risk Premium
questions.definition: Equity risk premium represents the excess return expected from equity over a risk-free return as compensation for equity risk.
questions.formula: Equity Risk Premium = Rx − Rf = βx(Rm − Rf)
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → give CAPM relationship → distinguish equity risk premium from market risk premium.

questions.question: Discount Rate
questions.definition: Discount rate is the rate used to convert future cash flows into present value and reflects risk-free return plus relevant risk premium.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain risk premium → explain why different cash flows can have different discount rates.

questions.question: Nominal Cash Flow versus Real Cash Flow
questions.definition: Nominal cash flows include inflation effects; real cash flows are stated after removing inflation effects.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → state consistency rule between cash flow and discount rate.

questions.question: Valuation of Equity Shares – Dividend, Earnings and Cash Flow Models
questions.definition: Equity can be valued using expected dividends, earnings multiples or expected cash flows, depending on the available information and valuation approach.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify model → state assumption → give key formula/logic → explain suitable application.

questions.question: Valuation of Preference Shares
questions.definition: Preference share valuation depends on the nature of dividend, redemption and other contractual cash flows.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify cash-flow pattern → discount dividends and redemption according to the relevant model.

questions.question: Valuation of Debentures/Bonds
questions.definition: Bond value is the present value of contractual interest/coupon payments plus redemption value discounted at the appropriate required return.
questions.answer_skeleton: Value periodic interest → value redemption → add present values.

questions.question: Role and Responsibilities of Valuers
questions.definition: A valuer provides an independent professional valuation while maintaining competence, due care, integrity, independence and confidentiality.
questions.answer_skeleton: State statutory valuation situations → explain professional responsibilities.

questions.question: Precautions before accepting a valuation assignment
questions.definition: A valuation is a professional estimate rather than an absolute number, so the valuer must understand the assignment, information, assumptions and potential conflicts before acceptance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain why valuation is an estimate → verify information → understand business → assess independence and assignment suitability.

chapters.title: Portfolio Management
chapters.memory_map: PROCESS → THEORY → RISK → REVISION → EVALUATION → ASSET ALLOCATION

questions.question: Portfolio Management Process
questions.definition: Portfolio management is a continuous process of selecting, combining, revising and evaluating securities to achieve the investor's risk-return objectives.
questions.answer_skeleton: Analyse → construct/select → revise → evaluate.

questions.question: Traditional Approach to Portfolio Management
questions.definition: Traditional portfolio management begins with understanding investor needs and then develops objectives, strategy, diversification and security selection.
questions.answer_skeleton: Know investor → define objective → strategy → diversify → select securities.

questions.question: Portfolio Rebalancing Policies
questions.definition: Portfolio rebalancing policies determine how asset proportions are changed when market values move or investor objectives change.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each policy → explain how allocation changes with market movements.

questions.question: Risk as an Integral Part of the Market
questions.definition: Market risk cannot be completely eliminated through diversification because systematic risk affects securities broadly.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain systematic risk → relate to market trends and indices.
questions.exam_trigger: Risk as integral part of market

questions.question: Portfolio Evaluation
questions.definition: Portfolio evaluation measures actual return relative to risk borne over a selected period and identifies weaknesses in investment performance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define evaluation → explain risk-adjusted performance measures.

questions.question: Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen Measures
questions.definition: These measures assess portfolio performance after adjusting returns for different measures of risk.
questions.memory_code: S = σ; T = β; J = α
questions.answer_skeleton: State each measure → identify risk measure → explain interpretation.

questions.question: Asset Allocation
questions.definition: Asset allocation determines how investment funds are distributed among asset classes according to return, risk, liquidity and investor objectives.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain strategic allocation → link with investor risk and return objectives.

questions.question: Alternative Investment Avenues
questions.definition: Alternative investments are non-traditional asset classes that can diversify portfolios beyond conventional securities.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name alternatives → explain diversification/liquidity/risk characteristics briefly.

chapters.title: Securitization
chapters.memory_map: MEANING → PARTICIPANTS → MECHANISM → INSTRUMENTS → BENEFITS/PROBLEMS → RISK → BLOCKCHAIN

questions.question: Meaning of Securitization
questions.definition: Securitization converts a pool of financial assets or receivables into marketable securities backed by the cash flows from those assets.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain conversion of illiquid receivables into tradable securities.

questions.question: Participants in Securitization
questions.definition: Securitization involves parties responsible for originating assets, structuring the transaction, transferring/holding assets, servicing, enhancing credit, rating and investing.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name participants → give one-line role of each.

questions.question: Mechanism of Securitization
questions.definition: The mechanism involves pooling receivables, transferring them to an SPV, issuing securities to investors and using underlying cash flows for repayment.
questions.answer_skeleton: Draw the flow and explain each stage.

questions.question: Features of Securitization
questions.definition: Securitization creates structured financial instruments by transforming pools of assets and their cash flows into securities with different risk/return characteristics.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each feature and its purpose.

questions.question: Benefits of Securitization
questions.definition: Securitization can convert receivables into liquidity and provide funding, risk-transfer and balance-sheet benefits.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain how originator obtains funds and how investors obtain asset-backed investment opportunities.

questions.question: Problems in Securitization in India
questions.definition: The development of securitization can be constrained by legal, tax, accounting, market and enforcement-related issues.
questions.answer_skeleton: Group problems into legal, tax, accounting, standardisation, market and enforcement categories.

questions.question: PTC versus Pay Through Security
questions.definition: PTCs pass underlying principal/interest collections through to investors, while pay-through structures issue securities whose payments can be structured differently from the timing of underlying collections.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → compare cash-flow timing and structuring.

questions.question: Pricing of Securitized Instruments
questions.definition: Pricing depends on the perspective of the originator and investor and the expected cash flows, risk and required return.
questions.answer_skeleton: Originator angle → amortise funding cost; investor angle → discount expected cash flows at comparable yield/YTM.

questions.question: Risks in Securitization
questions.definition: Securitization exposes investors and transaction participants to credit, legal and market risks.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each risk and explain its effect on pool cash flows or investor payouts.

questions.question: Blockchain Transaction and Risks
questions.definition: Blockchain is a distributed ledger system in which transactions are validated and recorded across a network rather than relying on a single central authority.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain blockchain mechanism → discuss technology, governance and information risks.

questions.question: Applications of Blockchain
questions.definition: Blockchain can be applied wherever shared, traceable and tamper-resistant transaction records are useful.
questions.answer_skeleton: List application sectors → explain the transaction-record benefit in each.

questions.question: Tokenization versus Securitization
questions.definition: Tokenization digitally represents assets as blockchain-based tokens, while securitization converts asset cash flows into structured marketable securities.
questions.memory_code: TOKEN = DIGITAL REPRESENTATION; SECURITIZATION = CASH-FLOW SECURITIES
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → compare structure → explain common benefits such as liquidity and tradability.

chapters.title: Mutual Funds
chapters.memory_map: MEANING → TYPES → EVALUATION → SIDE POCKET → TRACKING ERROR → ETF

questions.question: Special Categories of Mutual Funds
questions.definition: Special funds are schemes designed around a specific geography, sector, asset class, strategy or investment objective.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name category → explain its investment focus.

questions.question: Advantages and Disadvantages of Mutual Funds
questions.definition: Mutual funds pool investor money and professionally manage diversified portfolios, but involve costs, market risk and possible underperformance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Benefits → diversification/professional management/liquidity; drawbacks → fees, selection risk and market loss.

questions.question: Side Pocketing
questions.definition: Side pocketing separates stressed or illiquid assets from the liquid portfolio so that the affected investment can be isolated rather than forcing distress selling.
questions.memory_code: RISKY ASSET → SIDE POCKET → LIQUID NAV
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain separation → explain effect on NAV and investor liquidity.

questions.question: Tracking Error and its reasons
questions.definition: Tracking error is the deviation between a fund's return and the return of its benchmark.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define tracking error → explain five causes → lower tracking error means closer benchmark replication.

questions.question: Exchange Traded Fund (ETF)
questions.definition: An ETF combines features of an investment fund with exchange trading and is generally listed and traded during market hours.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define ETF → explain exchange listing, trading and authorised participants.

questions.question: Financial Evaluation Measures of Mutual Funds
questions.definition: Mutual fund performance can be assessed using risk-adjusted and cost-related measures.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each measure and state what risk/cost aspect it captures.

questions.question: Role of Fund Manager
questions.definition: The fund manager converts the scheme's stated objective into investment decisions while controlling risk, liquidity and portfolio composition.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain investment, risk, liquidity and monitoring responsibilities.

chapters.title: Derivatives Analysis and Valuation
chapters.memory_map: FORWARD → FUTURE → OPTION → GREEKS → EXOTIC → CREDIT → REAL → SWAP

questions.question: Meaning of Derivative
questions.definition: A derivative is a financial contract whose value is derived from one or more underlying assets, indices or reference rates.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → identify underlying → explain why change in underlying changes derivative value.

questions.question: Forward versus Futures
questions.definition: Both are contracts to transact an underlying at a future date, but futures are standardised and exchange-traded whereas forwards are generally customised OTC contracts.
questions.answer_skeleton: Compare standardisation, trading venue, settlement, margin and counterparty exposure.

questions.question: Pricing of Forwards and Futures
questions.definition: Forward/futures pricing is based on the relationship between spot value, carrying costs/benefits, financing and time to maturity.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain no-arbitrage logic → identify financing/carry and income effects.

questions.question: Hedging using Futures
questions.definition: Futures hedging reduces exposure to adverse price movements by taking an offsetting futures position.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify exposure → choose long/short hedge → explain offset → mention basis risk.

questions.question: Options
questions.definition: An option gives the buyer a right, but not an obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a specified strike price under stated contract conditions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → call vs put → buyer/seller rights and obligations → premium.

questions.question: Option Greeks
questions.definition: Greeks measure the sensitivity of option value to changes in key variables.

definitions.Delta: Sensitivity of option price to a change in underlying price.
definitions.Gamma: Sensitivity of delta to a change in underlying price.
definitions.Theta: Sensitivity of option value to passage of time.
definitions.Rho: Sensitivity of option value to interest-rate changes.
definitions.Vega: Sensitivity of option value to volatility changes.

questions.question: Exotic Options
questions.definition: Exotic options are option contracts with structures or payoff conditions different from standard plain-vanilla options.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define exotic option → name types → give one-line distinguishing feature.

questions.question: Credit Derivatives
questions.definition: Credit derivatives transfer or manage credit exposure using contracts whose value depends on credit events or credit-related underlying instruments.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain credit-risk transfer → mention relevant structures.

questions.question: Real Options
questions.definition: Real options recognise managerial flexibility embedded in investment projects, such as the ability to expand, delay, abandon or switch.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain why conventional NPV may omit managerial flexibility → identify option type.

questions.question: Derivative Mishaps and Lessons
questions.definition: Derivative failures demonstrate that leverage, model risk, inadequate controls, weak governance and misunderstood exposures can create large losses.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify source of failure → connect to risk-management lesson.

questions.question: Swaps
questions.definition: A swap is an agreement under which parties exchange specified cash-flow streams according to agreed terms.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain parties exchange cash flows → identify common swap types.

questions.question: Commodity, Weather and Electricity Derivatives
questions.definition: These derivatives use specialised physical or environmental variables as underlying references for hedging price, weather or power-related exposure.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify underlying → identify business exposure → explain hedging purpose.

chapters.title: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
chapters.memory_map: FX MARKET → RATE THEORIES → EXPOSURES → RISK MANAGEMENT → SWIFT/PAYMENTS

questions.question: Foreign Exchange Market
questions.definition: The foreign exchange market facilitates conversion and transfer of purchasing power from one currency into another.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define market → identify participants → explain currency conversion function.

questions.question: Factors affecting Exchange Rates
questions.definition: Exchange rates are influenced by economic, monetary, inflation, interest-rate, trade and market factors.
questions.answer_skeleton: List factors → explain how each can influence currency demand/supply.

questions.question: Interest Rate Parity (IRP)
questions.definition: IRP links the forward premium/discount of a currency with the interest-rate differential between two countries.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → state relationship → explain economic logic.

questions.question: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)
questions.definition: PPP links expected exchange-rate changes with differences in inflation rates between countries.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain inflation differential → state expected spot-rate implication.

questions.question: International Fisher Effect (IFE)
questions.definition: IFE links exchange-rate movements with interest-rate differentials, with higher nominal rates reflecting higher expected inflation.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → connect nominal interest differential with expected currency movement.

questions.question: Transaction Exposure
questions.definition: Transaction exposure measures the effect of exchange-rate changes on existing contractual foreign-currency cash flows that will be settled later.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → give importer/exporter example → explain gain/loss.

questions.question: Translation Exposure
questions.definition: Translation exposure arises when foreign-currency financial statements of subsidiaries are converted into the reporting currency for consolidation.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain consolidation impact.

questions.question: Economic Exposure
questions.definition: Economic exposure is the broader effect of exchange-rate changes on the economic value, competitive position, costs and revenues of the firm.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain long-term operating impact → distinguish from transaction and translation exposure.

questions.question: Foreign Exchange Risk Management
questions.definition: FX risk management identifies, measures and mitigates losses arising from currency fluctuations.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain why FX risk must be managed → connect to stability, cost, competitiveness, cash flow and compliance.

questions.question: Role of SWIFT
questions.definition: SWIFT provides a standardised communication network for transmitting financial messages between participating financial institutions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define SWIFT → explain messaging role → distinguish communication from actual settlement.

questions.question: National and International Payment Gateways
questions.definition: Payment gateways facilitate electronic payment instructions and processing across payment networks, supporting domestic and cross-border transactions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain the payment flow and cross-border relevance.

chapters.title: International Financial Management
chapters.memory_map: ICB → INTERNATIONAL FUNDS → SOVEREIGN FUNDS → GIFT CITY → CASH/RECEIVABLE/INVENTORY

questions.question: Complexities in International Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: International capital budgeting is more complex than domestic budgeting because project and parent cash flows, currencies, taxes, political risk and capital restrictions interact.
questions.answer_skeleton: Start with domestic vs international difference → explain each complexity.

questions.question: Offshore Investment Strategy versus Domestic Capital Budgeting
questions.definition: Offshore investment decisions require additional adjustments for currency, country, tax, political and transferability risks beyond domestic project evaluation.
questions.answer_skeleton: Compare common NPV framework with additional international adjustments.

questions.question: Project Cash Flow versus Parent Cash Flow
questions.definition: Project cash flows are generated by the foreign project, whereas parent cash flows reflect the amounts actually available to the parent after tax, remittance restrictions and currency effects.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → explain why parent receives a different economic cash flow.

questions.question: International Cash Management Objectives
questions.definition: International cash management seeks to minimise currency exposure and transaction costs while ensuring liquidity and optimal deployment of excess cash.
questions.memory_code: MIN FX + MIN CASH + MIN COST + OPTIMISE
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each objective.

questions.question: Centralised Cash Management
questions.definition: Centralised cash management coordinates cash across subsidiaries to reduce idle balances, improve netting and optimise funding/investment decisions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain centralisation → netting → lower idle cash → coordinated currency/funding decisions.

questions.question: Constituents of an International Financial Centre
questions.definition: An international financial centre requires financial infrastructure, stable governance, strategic location, skilled professionals and an enabling regulatory/economic environment.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain six constituents.

questions.question: Benefits of GIFT City/IFC
questions.definition: An international financial centre can attract global financial activity, specialised professionals and international transactions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each benefit.

questions.question: FCCBs – Advantages and Disadvantages
questions.definition: Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds are foreign-currency debt instruments carrying a conversion feature into equity under specified conditions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define FCCB → advantages → disadvantages.

questions.question: Salient Features of FCCBs
questions.definition: FCCBs are foreign-currency denominated convertible instruments subject to applicable issue and custody requirements.
questions.answer_skeleton: State features in bullet form.

questions.question: International Working Capital Management
questions.definition: International working capital management coordinates cash, receivables and inventory across countries while managing currency, tax, liquidity and country-specific factors.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain the three working-capital components and international complications.

chapters.title: Interest Rate Risk Management
chapters.memory_map: IRR TYPES → MEASUREMENT → ALM/FRA → FUTURES/OPTIONS/SWAPS → SWAPTION

questions.question: Types of Interest Rate Risk
questions.definition: Interest-rate risk arises when changes in market rates adversely affect earnings, asset/liability values or reinvestment outcomes.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define IRR → explain each type with one line.

questions.question: Measurement of Interest Rate Risk
questions.definition: Interest-rate risk must first be identified and quantified before appropriate hedging can be designed.
questions.answer_skeleton: State what each technique measures.

questions.question: Asset and Liability Management (ALM)
questions.definition: ALM is a comprehensive framework for managing the structure of assets and liabilities so that interest earnings are optimised within the institution's risk preference.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain asset/liability matching → discuss broader functions.

questions.question: Hedging Interest Rate Risk
questions.definition: Interest-rate hedging uses balance-sheet techniques and derivatives to reduce adverse effects of rate movements.
questions.answer_skeleton: Classify traditional and modern methods → explain each.

questions.question: Net Interest Position and Price Risk
questions.definition: Net interest position reflects exposure of interest earnings to rate movements; price risk arises when interest-sensitive assets are sold before maturity and market yields change.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → explain impact on earnings and market value.

questions.question: Forward Rate Agreement (FRA) Features
questions.definition: An FRA is an off-balance-sheet agreement that fixes an interest rate for a future borrowing/lending period on a notional principal.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain notional → settlement → hedging purpose.

questions.question: Interest Rate Swaption
questions.definition: A swaption is an option giving the holder the right to enter into an interest-rate swap under specified terms.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → call/put → tenor/premium → settlement.

chapters.title: Business Valuation
chapters.memory_map: ASSET → EARNING → CASH FLOW → CAPM/APT → RELATIVE → EVA/MVA/SVA → FAIR/DISTRESSED

questions.question: Approaches to Business Valuation
questions.definition: Business valuation can be performed through asset-based, earning-based and cash-flow-based approaches, supplemented by contemporary methods.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name three core approaches → explain what each considers.

questions.question: Asset-Based Valuation
questions.definition: Asset-based valuation estimates business value from the value of assets and liabilities rather than primarily from future earnings.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain three variants → state strengths and limitations.

questions.question: Earning-Based Valuation
questions.definition: Earning-based valuation estimates business value from maintainable earnings capitalised at an appropriate rate or through an earnings multiple.
questions.answer_skeleton: P/E approach → maintainable earnings → capitalisation approach.

questions.question: Cash Flow Based Valuation / DCF
questions.definition: Cash-flow valuation discounts future free cash flows and terminal value at an appropriate cost of capital.
questions.answer_skeleton: Forecast FCF → determine discount rate → terminal value → present value → interpret enterprise/equity value.

questions.question: CAPM in Business Valuation
questions.definition: CAPM links required return to risk-free return plus beta-adjusted market risk premium.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain CAPM → beta → required return → application in discount rate.

questions.question: Estimating Beta for Unlisted Companies
questions.definition: For an unlisted company, beta can be estimated using comparable listed companies, adjusting/de-gearing their beta for differences in capital structure.
questions.answer_skeleton: Select comparables → calculate asset beta → adjust → obtain beta for target → apply CAPM.

questions.question: Relative Valuation
questions.definition: Relative valuation estimates value using comparable companies and market-based multiples linked to relevant business drivers.
questions.answer_skeleton: Select comparables → identify driver → derive multiple → apply to target.

questions.question: Chop-Shop Method
questions.definition: The chop-shop approach values separate business segments using comparable industry capitalisation ratios and aggregates their theoretical values.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify segments → apply comparable ratios → calculate segment values → aggregate.

questions.question: EVA, MVA and SVA
questions.definition: These contemporary approaches assess value creation from operating returns, market value or shareholder-value drivers.
formulas: MVA = Current Market Value − Invested Capital
questions.memory_code: EVA = OPERATING VALUE; MVA = MARKET VALUE; SVA = SHAREHOLDER VALUE
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each → give formula where relevant → explain value-creation interpretation.

questions.question: Fair Value and Valuation Range
questions.definition: Fair value should be approached through appropriate valuation methods and assumptions; valuation often produces a range rather than a single unquestionable number.
questions.answer_skeleton: Use available methods → compare results → analyse assumptions → derive reasonable range.

questions.question: Going Concern versus Non-Going Concern Valuation
questions.definition: Going-concern valuation assumes the business continues operations; non-going-concern valuation focuses more on realisable asset values and liquidation outcomes.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → explain different valuation basis.

questions.question: Valuation of Distressed Companies
questions.definition: Distressed-company valuation must recognise financial distress, reduced future cash flows, asset realisation and uncertainty surrounding continuity.
questions.answer_skeleton: Identify distress → assess viability → value assets/cash flows appropriately.

questions.question: Valuation of Digital/Technology/Professional Firms
questions.definition: Businesses with significant intangible value may require drivers beyond traditional asset-based measures.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain why book assets may understate value → identify industry-specific drivers.

chapters.title: Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring
chapters.memory_map: WHY → FORM → FINANCE → DEFEND → DIVEST → OWNERSHIP → VALUE → CROSS-BORDER → SPAC

questions.question: Concept of Corporate Restructuring
questions.definition: Corporate restructuring involves major changes in operations, assets, financial structure or ownership to respond to strategic and market conditions.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → internal vs external restructuring → examples.

questions.question: Merger versus Acquisition versus Takeover
questions.definition: A merger combines entities into one; acquisition involves one entity obtaining another; takeover generally refers to obtaining control of a company.
questions.memory_code: MERGE = COMBINE; ACQUIRE = BUY; TAKEOVER = CONTROL
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each → distinguish legal/economic effect.

questions.question: Rationale for Mergers and Acquisitions
questions.definition: M&A may be undertaken to achieve strategic, operational, financial or market-related objectives.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each rationale and connect it with expected value creation.

questions.question: Forms of M&A
questions.definition: M&A structures differ according to the relationship between businesses and the legal/financial form of combination.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each form and give the underlying business relationship.

questions.question: Financial Framework of M&A
questions.definition: The financial framework evaluates purchase consideration, financing, expected synergy, value transfer and post-merger financial effects.
questions.answer_skeleton: Value target → determine consideration → select financing → assess synergy/value impact.

questions.question: Takeover Defensive Tactics
questions.definition: Defensive tactics are measures adopted by a target company to resist or make an unwanted takeover more difficult.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name defence → explain how it makes takeover less attractive/difficult.

questions.question: Reverse Merger
questions.definition: A reverse merger is a transaction structure in which the ownership/control or listing outcome is achieved through a merger that reverses the usual direction of acquisition/control.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain structure → state strategic use.

questions.question: Divestiture, Demerger and Equity Carve-Out
questions.definition: Divestiture reduces or separates a business/asset; demerger separates an undertaking into distinct entities; an equity carve-out involves selling a portion of a subsidiary/business equity to outside investors.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define each restructuring form → explain ownership/cash-flow consequences.

questions.question: Financial and Ownership Restructuring
questions.definition: Financial restructuring changes the financing/capital structure; ownership restructuring changes who owns or controls the business.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define both → explain MBO/LBO/going-private structures.

questions.question: Unlocking Value through M&A and Restructuring
questions.definition: Value unlocking seeks to improve business value by realising synergies, separating non-core assets, improving capital structure or improving strategic focus.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain how restructuring can release value from assets, operations and ownership.

questions.question: Reasons for M&A Failure
questions.definition: M&A may fail when expected synergies or strategic benefits are not achieved or integration and valuation assumptions prove incorrect.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain financial, strategic and human/integration causes.

questions.question: Cross-Border Mergers
questions.definition: Cross-border mergers combine businesses across countries and therefore require consideration of currency, tax, regulatory, political and cultural issues.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain additional international complexities.

questions.question: SPACs
questions.definition: A Special Purpose Acquisition Company is formed to raise capital through a public vehicle with the purpose of subsequently acquiring or combining with a target business.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define SPAC → explain structure → explain acquisition/listing mechanism.

chapters.title: Startup Finance
chapters.memory_map: RECOGNITION → UNICORN → FUNDING → BOOTSTRAP → ANGEL → VC → EXIT → PITCH → SUCCESSION → VALUATION

questions.question: Startup Recognition Criteria
questions.definition: Startup recognition depends on prescribed legal/entity, age, turnover and innovation/development-related criteria under the applicable framework.
questions.answer_skeleton: State the recognition criteria in the applicable ICAI study framework.

questions.question: Unicorn Startup
questions.definition: A unicorn is a privately held startup reaching a valuation of at least US$1 billion.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define unicorn → distinguish decacorn → mention valuation nature.

questions.question: Innovative Sources of Startup Funding
questions.definition: Startups can use non-traditional funding sources in addition to conventional debt/equity finance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name source → explain how it provides early-stage liquidity/capital.

questions.question: Bootstrapping
questions.definition: Bootstrapping means financing and growing the startup primarily through internal resources and operating arrangements rather than external equity funding.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain methods → link to reduced external funding dependence.

questions.question: Angel Investors
questions.definition: Angel investors are individuals who invest their own money in early-stage businesses, usually in exchange for equity or convertible instruments.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define → explain investment form → investor expectation/exit.

questions.question: Characteristics of Venture Capital
questions.definition: Venture capital is long-term risk capital invested in high-growth businesses, generally with an equity participation and limited liquidity.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain four characteristics.

questions.question: VC Fund Structure in India
questions.definition: VC fund structures may be organised through domestic, offshore or unified structures depending on the funding and investment arrangement.
questions.answer_skeleton: Name structures → explain basic structural distinction.

questions.question: Tag-Along Clause and Exit Plan
questions.definition: A tag-along provision protects an investor by allowing it to participate in a sale of shares by specified existing shareholders, subject to agreed terms.
questions.answer_skeleton: Define clause → explain investor protection → list exit routes.

questions.question: Startup Risk Matrix / Funding Stages
questions.definition: Startup risk generally changes across funding stages as the business develops and uncertainty reduces.
questions.answer_skeleton: State the risk progression used in the study framework and connect it with maturity/funding stage.

questions.question: Startup Pitch Presentation
questions.definition: A startup pitch communicates the business opportunity, solution, market, team, model, financial prospects and funding requirement to potential investors.
questions.answer_skeleton: Introduce → team → problem → solution → market → projections → competition → model → financing.

questions.question: Business Succession Strategy
questions.definition: Succession strategy prepares the organisation to maintain leadership and critical capabilities when key individuals leave or roles change.
questions.answer_skeleton: Assess leadership needs → map competencies → identify gaps → develop/appoint successor.

questions.question: Need for Succession Planning
questions.definition: Succession planning reduces disruption by preparing talent for critical positions and maintaining continuity.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain continuity, risk reduction, talent development and conflict management.

questions.question: Venture Capital Valuation
questions.definition: The venture-capital method estimates the required future value and discounts it using an investor's target return or applies an investment multiple.
questions.memory_code: FUTURE EXIT → TARGET RETURN → PRESENT VALUE
questions.answer_skeleton: Estimate future exit value → apply required multiple/return → discount to present value.

questions.question: Berkus Approach
questions.definition: The Berkus approach values an early-stage startup using qualitative/early business-value factors rather than relying only on historical financial performance.
questions.answer_skeleton: Explain each value driver and how it contributes to startup valuation.
